claim: Pseudomonas fluorescens SBW25 growing in static broth microcosms rapidly depletes available oxygen establishing selective conditions that favour mutants able to colonise the air-liquid interface.
source: Pseudomonas fluorescens SBW25 growing in static broth microcosms rapidly depletes available oxygen establishing selective conditions that favour mutants able to colonise the air-liquid interface.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work (Ferguson et al., 2013; Lind et al., 2017b) and represents established knowledge about the experimental system.

claim: The most successful mutant-class encompasses the WS types.
source: The most successful mutant-class encompasses the WS types (Ferguson et al., 2013; Lind et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 2013 and Lind et al., 2017b.

claim: WS types arise from mutational activation of diguanylate cyclases (DGCs) that cause over-production of the second messenger c-di-GMP.
source: These types arise from mutational activation of diguanylate cyclases (DGCs) that cause over-production of the second messenger c-di-GMP (Goymer et al., 2006; McDonald et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goymer et al., 2006 and McDonald et al., 2009.

claim: Over-production of c-di-GMP leads to over-production of an acetylated cellulose polymer.
source: over-production of an acetylated cellulose polymer (Spiers et al., 2002; Spiers et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Spiers et al., 2002 and 2003.

claim: Over-production of cellulose ultimately leads to formation of a self-supporting microbial mat.
source: over-production of an acetylated cellulose polymer (Spiers et al., 2002; Spiers et al., 2003) and ultimately formation of a self-supporting microbial mat (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A showing the mat formation.

claim: Each time the tape of WS evolution is re-run mutations generating the adaptive type arise in one of three DGC-encoding pathways (Wsp, Aws, or Mws).
source: McDonald et al. (McDonald et al., 2009) showed that each time the tape of WS evolution is re-run mutations generating the adaptive type arise in one of three DGC-encoding pathways (Wsp, Aws, or Mws) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McDonald et al., 2009 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: When the three pathways (Wsp, Aws, Mws) are eliminated from the ancestral type evolution proceeds along multiple new pathways.
source: Subsequent work revealed that when these three pathways are eliminated from the ancestral type evolution proceeds along multiple new pathways (Lind et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lind et al., 2015.

claim: WS types arising via alternative pathways have fitnesses indistinguishable from those arising via mutations in Wsp, Aws, or Mws.
source: resulting in WS types whose fitnesses are indistinguishable from those arising via mutations in Wsp, Aws, or Mws.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lind et al., 2015 in the preceding sentence.

claim: Parallel evolution of WS involving preferential usage of the Wsp, Aws and Mws pathways is not explained by selection.
source: Parallel evolution of WS involving preferential usage of the Wsp, Aws and Mws pathways is therefore not explained by selection
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the previous findings about fitness equivalence and citation to Lind et al., 2015.

claim: Repeated use of Wsp, Aws and Mws stems from the fact that these pathways are subject to negative regulation and thus present a large mutational target.
source: repeated use of Wsp, Aws and Mws stems from the fact that these pathways are subject to negative regulation and thus, relative to pathways subject to positive regulation, or requiring promoter-activating mutations, gene fusion events, or other rare mutations, present a large mutational target (Lind et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lind et al., 2015.

claim: The mutation rate was highest for the Aws pathway (6.5 × 10−9).
source: The mutation rate was highest for the Aws pathway (6.5 × 10−9); approximately double that of Wsp (3.7 × 10−9) and an order of magnitude higher than that of the Mws pathway (0.74 × 10−9) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The mutation rate for the Wsp pathway is approximately 3.7 × 10−9.
source: The mutation rate was highest for the Aws pathway (6.5 × 10−9); approximately double that of Wsp (3.7 × 10−9) and an order of magnitude higher than that of the Mws pathway (0.74 × 10−9) (Figure 2).

claim: The mutation rate for the Mws pathway is 0.74 × 10−9.

claim: The rate at which WS mutants arose from the ancestral genotype in which the three pathways are intact (11.2 × 10−9) was approximately the sum of the rates for the three pathways (11.0 × 10−9).

claim: The Wsp, Aws and Mws pathways are the primary routes by which WS types evolve.

claim: The Aws pathway having the greatest capacity to generate WS is surprising given the smaller target size (three genes and 2.3 kb compared to seven genes (8.4 kb) in the Wsp pathway).
